title: Trees: terminology, representations and traversals
learningObjectives: Explain the topic and its C rules.
Trace the example and explain its data or control flow.
Identify edge cases and resource-management requirements.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: A tree consists of nodes connected by parent-child relationships. Common terms include root, leaf, parent, child, depth and height. Binary trees can be represented with linked nodes or arrays for suitable shapes; traversals include preorder, inorder and postorder.
understand.whyItMatters: Tree representations and traversal order determine how hierarchical data is stored and processed.
understand.analogy: Treat each algorithm or resource as a contract whose invariants must remain true after every operation.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal rules for pointers, object lifetime, complexity or library contracts.

explain.narrative:
A tree consists of nodes connected by parent-child relationships. Common terms include root, leaf, parent, child, depth and height. Binary trees can be represented with linked nodes or arrays for suitable shapes; traversals include preorder, inorder and postorder.

State preconditions, invariants, empty and full cases, ownership and failure behaviour before implementation. Compile with warnings and test normal, boundary and failure paths.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: Inorder traversal visits the left subtree, current node and right subtree. The callback receives each key; the function assumes the tree is valid and acyclic.

practise.guidedTask: Trace preorder, inorder and postorder on a three-node tree.
practise.independentTask: Implement all three traversals and test an empty tree, a single node and an unbalanced tree.
hints: Recursive traversal uses call-stack space proportional to tree height.
A malformed cyclic pointer structure can make traversal fail to terminate.
Define ownership and cleanup for every dynamically allocated node.
